report:
## Conclusion

**No — arthroscopic surgery does not meaningfully help knee osteoarthritis, and most current guidelines recommend against it.**

Multiple high-quality randomized, placebo-controlled trials have tested arthroscopic debridement/lavage for knee osteoarthritis against sham surgery or non-operative care. Moseley et al.'s landmark placebo-controlled trial found that outcomes after arthroscopic debridement or lavage were no better than after a sham surgical procedure at any point up to two years (NEJM, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259). A subsequent randomized trial by Kirkley et al. in patients with moderate-to-severe osteoarthritis similarly found no significant benefit of arthroscopic surgery plus physical/medical therapy over physical/medical therapy alone for pain or function (NEJM, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0708333).

A 2015 systematic review and meta-analysis in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, pooling trial data on degenerative knee disease (including osteoarthritis), concluded that arthroscopy produces only small, short-lived pain benefits that do not persist beyond 3 months, offers no functional improvement, and carries real risks (infection, DVT); the authors stated the findings "do not support the practise of arthroscopic surgery" in these patients (https://bjsm.bmj.com/content/49/19/1229).

Based on this evidence, the BMJ Rapid Recommendations panel (2017) issued a strong recommendation against arthroscopy for degenerative knee disease, including osteoarthritis with or without meniscal tears (https://www.bmj.com/content/357/bmj.j1982). NICE guidance similarly discourages routine knee arthroscopic washout/debridement for osteoarthritis.

**Bottom line:** For degenerative knee osteoarthritis, arthroscopic debridement/lavage offers no lasting pain or functional benefit beyond placebo or conservative treatment and exposes patients to surgical risks; it is not recommended except in select cases with concurrent mechanical symptoms (e.g., loose bodies) where clinical judgment may still favor limited use.
